title: When the Portrait Turns
premise: Isandro Underhill, a pest controller who has spent fifteen years rationalizing the unexplainable, is summoned to Hollowmere House to deal with 'something with fingerprints' — and finds her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on the porch, unchanged after two decades. The house's portraits turn their heads when unobserved, and each one hums a fragment of an old lullaby whose final verse, if sung by a living voice, will free the family trapped inside the paint — or bind Isandro among them. As she uncovers that her mother once escaped the same bargain and that Wren is the house's warden wearing a child's face, Isandro must choose between loyalty to the friend who protected her and the truth of what he really is. In the end she sings the last verse not as surrender but as a renaming, breaking the song's power and leaving Wren — freed, mortal, and fading — to choose his own ending.
about_author: Emrys Sterling is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing estate sales in decaying English manors, where the portraits never quite faced the walls. They write horror about houses that remember, and they still refuse to hang anything framed above eye level.

chapters.title: The Call with Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. A routine pest-control call describes smudges at impossible heights; Isandro takes it because the address is Hollowmere House, which she has avoided for fifteen years. The beat is dread disguised as professionalism — she tells herself it's just a job, while packing salt she pretends is for slugs.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Arriving at dusk, she finds a small boy on the porch steps — Wren, her childhood imaginary friend, exactly as he was at seven. He says only, 'You came back late.' The beat is vertigo: fifteen years of rational explanations collapse in a single sentence.

chapters.title: Hollowmere's Tenants
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Inside, the client, Mrs. Aldous, shows her the portrait gallery where every frame hangs slightly askew and every face has turned since yesterday. Fingerprints climb the wallpaper in ascending spirals. The beat is creeping wrongness — the house is inhabited, and politely so.

chapters.title: Explanations, Fifteen Years Deep
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, with flashbacks to age nine. She catalogs her old coping mechanisms — drafts, raccoons, carbon monoxide — trying to explain Wren away. He watches her do it with patient sadness. The beat is self-betrayal: she realizes the explanations were always for her mother's sake, not her own.

chapters.title: The Song in the Walls
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At 3 a.m., a lullaby seeps through the plaster, one verse per room, growing fuller as she moves toward the gallery. She recognizes it — her mother sang it before she vanished from Isandro's life. The beat is grief resurfacing as terror.

chapters.title: What the Portraits Remember
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous's POV. The elderly owner confesses the house has kept her family for six generations: relatives who 'went into the frames' rather than die elsewhere. She hired Isandro not for pests but because outsiders can hear the last verse without being claimed. The beat is complicity revealed.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, first time. He explains the terms: the house feeds on sung verses; each portrait hums its share; a living voice completing the song frees everyone — or joins them forever. He made himself her friend long ago to keep her from singing along as a child. The beat is tenderness with teeth.

chapters.title: Fingerprints at the Door
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The smudges begin appearing on the inside of doors she's locked, then on her own toolkit, then on her wrist — small, five-fingered, warm. Something in the house wants to be touched back. The beat is intimacy curdling into violation.

chapters.title: Mother's Verse
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, flashbacks interleaved. Searching the attic, she finds her mother's journal: her mother grew up in Hollowmere, learned three verses, and fled mid-song, leaving her own sister behind in a frame. The beat is inheritance — Isandro was always coming back here.

chapters.title: The Aunt in the Gilt Frame
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In the gallery she finds a portrait of a woman with her own jawline, humming the third verse in perfect sync with the walls. Her aunt speaks one word through the canvas: 'Finish.' The beat is temptation — freedom offered in a voice like family.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Price
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren admits he lied: he isn't her imagination given form; he's the house's first victim, reshaped into a warden, and keeping Isandro safe meant keeping her ignorant. Mrs. Aldous overhears. The beat is betrayal — love built on a managed truth.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Sings
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Desperate to join her husband in the frames, Mrs. Aldous begins the fourth verse at midnight. Wren smothers the sound; the house retaliates, turning every portrait toward Isandro's bedroom door. The beat is escalation — the house has chosen its singer.

chapters.title: Invisible No Longer
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The fingerprints now spell her name on the ceiling above her bed. She understands: staying invisible — to the house, to her past, to herself — was never an option. The beat is acceptance, cold and clarifying.

chapters.title: The Gallery at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At dawn the portraits are at their weakest, faces slack. She walks the gallery mapping verses to frames, learning who hums what, and discovers a blank canvas at the corridor's end — freshly primed, sized for her. The beat is grim resolve sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Verse Against Verse
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Isandro attempts to sing the fifth verse backward, unraveling the song; the house counters by giving Wren her mother's voice. Torn between the melody and the mimicry, she falters — and the blank canvas begins to fill with her outline. The beat is the midpoint collapse.

chapters.title: What Wren Was Before
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Through the house's memory, Isandro sees him as he was: a groundskeeper's son, first singer, first prisoner, carved into a child's shape because children are trusted. The beat is devastating compassion — her oldest friend is the house's oldest wound.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Written Down
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Her aunt's portrait weeps turpentine; beneath the frame, scratched into the wall, is the final verse in her mother's handwriting — unfinished, the last line torn away. The beat is hope with a hole in it: the answer exists but refuses to be whole.

chapters.title: Sacrifice Offered
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous's POV. The old woman offers Isandro a trade: let the house take her instead, and it will release the Underhill bloodline entirely. Isandro nearly accepts — duty dressed as love — until she sees Mrs. Aldous's hands already translucent. The beat is the loyalty-versus-truth theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Renaming
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, climax. In the gallery at midnight, all twenty-two portraits singing, Isandro completes the verse — but changes the final line, renaming the house's captive dead instead of invoking them. The song breaks mid-note; frames crack; the blank canvas splits down the middle. The beat is triumph achieved through refusal, not compliance.

chapters.title: Wren, Unbound
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Freed from wardenship, Wren becomes mortal and begins aging rapidly, decades owed arriving at once. He asks Isandro whether he was ever real or only useful. She answers with the truth: both, and both were enough. The beat is love against duty, resolved honestly.

chapters.title: Empty Frames
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The portraits are vacant now, the dead gone wherever renamed things go. Mrs. Aldous, spared but alone, chooses to stay in the quiet house. Isandro packs her tools, leaves the salt, and locks nothing. The beat is bittersweet aftermath — freedom leaves its own silence.

chapters.title: The Song's Last Verse, Unwritten
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, epilogue. Months later, a new client calls about humming in their walls. On the porch of their house waits no one — but in her truck's mirror, briefly, a young man waves, aged right, smiling, gone. Isandro drives on, humming nothing. The beat is closure with an open window: some songs end; some just change singers.
